title_en: He Gave the Vaishnavs Water to Drink
translation:
_Kunvarbai jab kahi nishani, kyari manse tum paayo paani_ (Kunvarbai then gave the sign, saying: "You gave water within the furrow-bed.") (from Gnan Mahima)

Once there was a festival (ochhav) in another village (Ori Gaudi - Kasampur). Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj was travelling in a bullock-cart together with the child-devotees (bal gopal), singing bhajans and kirtans along the way. On the road the sants and children became extremely thirsty, and the small children began to cry loudly. Then one sant ran ahead and had all the carts (the covered bullock-carts, damaniyan velo) halted. Seeing some shade, everyone stopped there and gathered together. Jivanji Maharaj welcomed them lovingly. Then Kunvarbai said, "Antaryami (indwelling knower of every heart) Sadguru, listen: everyone is very thirsty, water is not to be found anywhere, so please find some way." Jivanji Maharaj got down from the cart. Kunvarbai then said, "When you took the Krishna-avatar and were sporting as a cowherd grazing cattle on Govardhan hill, the gopis and cowherds had all gathered there, and at that time they had become extremely thirsty. Then you lifted up a clod of earth (dhekun) and gave everyone water to drink. Since you are capable of such things, give us water to drink now too, by whatever means." Then, going to a low-lying spot where the ground had dried and cracked open, Jivanji Maharaj lifted up a mound of earth; at once water welled up and filled the place. He told everyone to quickly drink water from that pit. Everyone first gave Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj water to drink, then they drank themselves, and everyone also filled their own vessels with water. Then Jivanji Maharaj covered the mound back over, and the ground became as dry as it had been before. All the sants bowed at Jivanji Maharaj's feet. Then they reached the village of Ori.

From the village all the sants came out to meet him, playing the kansi, taal and mridang (cymbals and drum), and bowed in prostration before Jivanji Maharaj. Then, just as when Ramchandra, having brought Sitaji back from Lanka, returned to Ayodhya, and Bharatji together with the people of Ayodhya went out with music and celebration to welcome Ram, Lakshman, Bharat and Hanuman, Bhandas composed a hymn (pad) describing that occasion.

Singing that very hymn, they brought Jivanji Maharaj into the village with music and festivity, ceremonially welcoming him (padharamani). We still sing that hymn today on the occasion of a guru's ceremonial arrival. This hymn was probably being sung even in Jivanji Maharaj's own lifetime, because it is mentioned in the parcharee (the traditional account of his life and wonders) of Jivanji Maharaj, and that proves it. So this hymn has been in use in our community since ancient times, and its importance is all the greater for that reason.

_Aavu rudu ne rasalu re, aavya ayodhyaman ramji re || Praja te lei bharat parharya re, harina vadan nihalu re || Aavya ||_ (How lovely and delightful — Ramji has come to Ayodhya! Taking the people with him, Bharat went out to receive him, saying, "Let me behold the Lord's face." — He has come.)

In our community, the greatest special quality compared to other communities is that on every occasion our devotees send for their guru and welcome him ceremonially with due honor. This is not seen anywhere in any community but our own; rarely, only once in a while, do people elsewhere send for their guru, whereas we always send for the guru first, welcome him ceremonially, and only then begin to celebrate any occasion at all. Moreover, the meal-offering (bhojan prasad) too is served in the row of diners (pangat) only after the guru has offered the rosary (mala) to it, in a disciplined manner; and while it is being served, everyone together calls out "Aad," and only when Jivanji Maharaj's jai (victory-cry) is raised does everyone eat the meal-prasad, saying "Ramkabir." Such a disciplined practice is not found anywhere else. In this way Jivanji Maharaj has made our community fully virtuous and disciplined in every respect.

Offering the rosary to the food before it is eaten is also our distinctive practice, and even at ordinary festivals, the meal-prasad is given only after a tulsi leaf has been offered near the devotee of the household shrine (parthara). Another feature that is astonishing about our community is this: on any occasion — whether we gather for bhajan-kirtan and bhakti at Ram-Janma or Krishna-Janma or any other festival, where devotional hymns being sung is only natural — even at a wedding, a death, a farewell occasion (aana-tanaa), a house-warming, or any other kind of occasion, we sing nothing but devotional bhajan-kirtans. So for us a wedding is not merely a wedding but an occasion for bhajan-kirtan, and we treat every such occasion purely as an occasion for bhajan. Hence even at our weddings, wedding songs are sung, but among them nothing but devotional songs to Ram or Krishna are sung, never other wedding ditties or ordinary wedding songs. This is why it is no failing at all that the devotee community records its surname as "Bhagat" (devotee). We truly are practicers of devotion, so it is not out of place that our surname should be Bhagat; we are not devotees in name only but true practicers of devotion, and so we fully deserve, in the truest sense, the surname of Bhagat. The sad thing is that when our community sees other, worldly communities and, drawn toward them, imitates their ways, that tarnishes our worthiness. We have never considered even the occasion of death inauspicious; so although it is a sorrowful occasion, we do not create an atmosphere heavy with excessive grief, but only do bhajan-kirtan. Just as we make a sukhadi meal-offering at birth and at the thread-initiation (kanthi diksha), so too at a death we distribute sukhadi as prasad. This is because we say that death is not death but hari-sharan, having taken refuge in the Lord. Furthermore, even in everyday speech we use these cultural terms: jal instead of paani (water), prasad instead of khavu (eating), hari-sharan instead of maran (death), and so on. In no community but ours is it ever possible to sing devotional wedding-songs at a wedding, whereas for us it is never possible to sing anything at a wedding but devotional songs. So if someone in another community were to sing our wedding song, which is a devotional hymn, at their wedding the way we do, it would not seem fitting to that community, and they would feel in their minds, "We have gathered for a wedding now, we have not come for a bhajan program." But when we sing these very hymns on a wedding occasion, no such hesitation whatsoever arises in anyone's mind. That is precisely why, though we are devotees, we are truly exceptional, unparalleled Vaishnavs.

A true Vaishnav is not a hypocrite or a fraud, so we do not put on false show. Jivanji Maharaj never expressed any sense of pride in being a guru. He was the founder of the Uda path (the true devotees' path) and the giver of true devotion, so he never engaged in outward pomp or showy display. Yet today we have fallen into the error of hypocrisy and false conduct. People may well have bowed at Jivanji Maharaj's feet, but it is never written or heard anywhere that anyone, at any place, washed his feet and took that foot-water (charanamrut) with special honor. This excess of outward show is shameful. Moreover, cloth is considered valuable, and yet to spread it in dusty roads and lanes in order to welcome the guru with special honor is entirely improper. To welcome the guru ceremonially while playing kansi, taal and mridang and singing kirtan is fitting, but to hold up an umbrella and spread out cloths even when there is no sun is a false display and is laughable. Looking through the Illustrated Life-Episodes of Jivanji Maharaj, Part 3, it is clear that compassionate Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj showered nothing but grace for the love and devotion of his devotees. On the way to Ori village, Kasampur, past Ganpatpura, between there and Kurali, there is a small pond, which still exists today. There, we too have often given water to thirsty bullocks. So it must have been right at this very pond that Sadguru Jivanji gave water to these thirsty child-gopal-sants. And so this pond, even today, is a place that recalls Jivanji Maharaj to memory.
